A neuromorphic architecture simulator, NESA, has been developed to efficiently simulate neuromorphic systems with memristive devices.  NESA's core consists of a Python-based software that integrates a fast, time-stepping solver, models of individual memristive devices, and a range of neuromorphic architectures.  This simulator enables researchers to examine and compare various memristive devices and architectures in a unified framework, and to test different neuromorphic architectures incorporating diverse memristive devices.  NESA's capabilities are demonstrated through simulations of a specific memristive device and a particular neuromorphic architecture, and it is shown to be applicable to a wide variety of memristive devices and architectures.  NESA's source code and documentation are available for public access.  This work highlights the potential of NESA to facilitate the development and optimization of memristive devices and architectures for neuromorphic applications.  NESA's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/berkeleylab/nesa.  A related video demonstration can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qhj2s2z2sA0. We present a novel approach called Reward-Biased Maximum Likelihood Estimation for contextual reinforcement learning agents. By decoupling the learning process, this method enables the agent to learn a policy that prioritizes high-reward interactions and a value function that accurately reflects the agent's likelihood of achieving those rewards. This separation allows for a more efficient and effective learning process, where the agent can focus on optimal reward interactions without being hindered by suboptimal exploration. In our implementation, RBMLE is combined with an actor-critic algorithm that leverages a global value function to guide exploration and policy learning. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can learn more efficient policies and value functions compared to standard maximum likelihood estimation, even in large-scale, multi-task environments. Furthermore, our method can be integrated with other biasing techniques to achieve superior outcomes. For example, by incorporating a prior bias, our agent can achieve exceptional performance in a challenging, multi-task environment. Additionally, our method can be combined with a curiosity-driven approach to achieve outstanding performance in a variety of environments. Overall, our findings suggest that RBMLE can lead to more efficient learning and improved performance in contextual reinforcement learning algorithms. The art of video editing is a complex process that involves a range of
technical and artistic decisions. Despite the difficulty of replicating it with
artificial intelligence, there has been significant progress in recent years. A
key factor in this advancement has been the development of large datasets
containing extensive information about the video editing process. However,
there has been limited research into the fundamental structure of video
editing, and how it differs across various datasets. To address this knowledge
gap, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of 1,171 films, which provides
a wealth of information about the video editing structure. This dataset has been
used to create a benchmark suite consisting of 13 tasks that test AI
performance in understanding and replicating video editing patterns. We have
also developed a new evaluation metric that takes into account the video
cutting and insertion techniques used in film editing. Experiments on our
benchmark suite have shown that the current state-of-the-art AI models still
fall short of human editing capabilities, highlighting the need for further
research in this area. Our dataset and benchmark are now available for
download at: https://sites.google.com/view/video-editing-dataset/. The
associated code can be accessed at

Our comprehensive study of single-hole spin dynamics in semiconductor quantum dots reveals the significance of spin-related interactions in these systems. We have developed a precise and efficient numerical method to simulate the accurate control of single-hole spins in solid-state environments. Our approach, which involves solving the time-convolutionless master equation, accurately captures the system's behavior under realistic conditions. We have applied this method to a GaAs quantum dot, where the bi-linear spin-orbit interaction plays a crucial role. Our findings show that the spin decay time can be prolonged by adjusting the system parameters, and we have identified the optimal conditions for maintaining coherence in the bi-linear spin-orbit interaction regime. Our study provides a foundation for the accurate simulation of spin dynamics in semiconductor quantum dots under realistic conditions. We anticipate that our results will contribute to the development of reliable spin-based technologies. In this research, we introduce Rand-OFDM, a secure wireless communication system built on a traditional OFDM framework. By randomly shifting the frequency domain OFDM bins within a predefined range, we ensure that even with full knowledge of the channel, an unauthorized receiver cannot accurately decode the transmitted data. Furthermore, we establish that the required shift size must exceed a specific threshold to guarantee system reliability. Our analysis also reveals that the performance of Rand-OFDM is comparable to that of standard OFDM when the system is securely operated below this threshold. Moreover, we demonstrate that even if the system is compromised, its security is not compromised, a first in wireless communication systems. Finally, we investigate the required system settings to achieve secure operation, taking into account factors like system noise and desired data recovery rates. Simulation results based on Rand-OFDM demonstrate its feasibility and effectiveness in real-world applications. Our study also includes a Python implementation of Rand-OFDM for practical use. This study introduces a novel approach to visual object detection in documents by leveraging a generative model that captures the inherent structure within images. The proposed method employs a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to learn the spatial relationships between visual objects in an image. By training the cGAN on a dataset of images with annotated objects, the network can generate a synthetic image containing the objects of interest. The cGAN model was evaluated on a dataset of document images containing text and graphic objects, and was compared to traditional object detection methods based on region proposal networks (RPNs). The results demonstrate that the cGAN model achieves comparable performance to RPN-based methods for text detection in documents, and superior performance for detecting graphic objects in documents. The proposed method's ability to generate synthetic images containing the objects of interest enables the detection of visual objects in documents. This study aims to develop an efficient method for deriving the best control strategies
for complex systems that can handle various types of nonlinearity and dynamic changes.
To achieve this goal, the control laws will be formulated as machine-learning models,
specifically as deep neural networks, which can effectively capture non-linear patterns and
dynamics in the system. To ensure the optimal performance of these control laws, the
training process will be designed to maximize a specific performance metric using a
reinforcement learning approach. To validate the effectiveness of this method, the trained
control laws will be tested on a challenging control problem involving an underactuated
double-integrator system, where the results will be evaluated against optimal control theory
and verified through numerical simulations. Ultimately, the feasibility and effectiveness of
this method will be compared to conventional control approaches in terms of its ability to
create robust and optimal control strategies for complex systems. To facilitate practical
implementation, the proposed method will be demonstrated using a physical robotic setup.

To address this issue, we have developed a novel video modelling framework that leverages the efficiency of traditional video models by utilizing a large-scale video encoder. This approach enables the model to process video data at higher resolutions while maintaining improved performance. To achieve this, we have designed a new video forward-transmission framework that efficiently handles large-scale video data. The framework consists of a gradient-based module that reduces video resolution to a compact size, and a loss-based module that combines multiple tasks into a single unified loss function. This allows for the efficient training of large-scale video models. Furthermore, we have introduced a new video encoder that can handle high-resolution video data, and developed a large-scale video model that demonstrates superior performance on various video understanding tasks. Experimental results show that our framework achieves state-of-the-art results on several video understanding benchmarks. The proposed video encoder also outperforms other models in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. The copyright issue in the machine learning industry remains unresolved, as existing solutions for dataset copyright protection are vulnerable to attacks and may compromise model performance. To address this problem, we introduce a novel, untargeted backdoor watermark approach that is both robust and efficient. This method embeds a robust watermark in a machine learning model, allowing it to detect the unauthorized use of protected datasets, even when transformed or perturbed. Our untargeted watermark approach is designed to withstand various attacks and data manipulations, while minimizing the impact on model performance. To verify its effectiveness, we conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets and models, and our results demonstrate that the watermarked model can maintain at least 90% of its original accuracy. Furthermore, we validated the robustness of the watermark by simulating various attacks and demonstrating its ability to identify unauthorized use of the protected dataset. Notably, our approach is the first to achieve both robustness and efficiency. Compared to existing solutions, our untargeted watermark approach offers improved robustness against attacks and data manipulations, and it does not require any prior knowledge of the dataset used to build the model. The code for this method is available at https://github.com/ChenCheng1996/Untargeted_Backdoor_Watermark. Overall, our work paves the way for a practical dataset copyright protection system. The Semantic Web's core language, RDF, has been enhanced to represent a scene graph (RG) of interconnected objects within an environment. This concept, known as the Web of Visual Objects (WoVO), leverages Visual Scene Graph (VG) to integrate a range of visual elements into the traditional Web. However, existing query languages like SPARQL struggle to accommodate the diverse features of RGs, limiting their effectiveness in multimodal applications. To address this, we propose VGStore, a new language that builds upon SPARQL to support visual scene graph queries and multimodal query composition. By providing a comprehensive framework for VG query processing, VGStore enables users to query and retrieve relevant visual information. In our evaluation, VGStore outperforms SPARQL in query answering and demonstrates its superiority over combined SPARQL-VG approaches. Notably, our results show that VGStore can efficiently handle complex queries with 10-20 variables and 10-20 visual elements in under 10ms. The source code for VGStore is available online. We plan to integrate it into the existing SPARQL databases, such as DBpedia and Wikidata, and to develop a Visual Scene Graph database for further research. The competition between alpha-decay and spontaneous fission is a crucial aspect in the study of alpha-decay chains of superheavy nuclei. Deep neural networks have achieved impressive success in various fields, yet their performance remains uncertain. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive explanation for the exceptional capabilities of deep learning. By revisiting the fundamental concept of interpolation and model complexity, we will demonstrate how it can be applied to multiple areas within the field of deep learning. We will examine how interpolation can be used to (i) explain the remarkable success of overparameterized models, such as neural networks and Gaussian processes, with infinite parameters; (ii) understand the role of data diversity in ensuring generalizability; (iii) address the phenomenon of catastrophic (un)learning; and (iv) comprehend the theoretical foundations of deep learning. By doing so, we will reveal that these seemingly unrelated phenomena are, in fact, interconnected aspects of the same underlying principle of interpolation. This paper is intended for readers who are new to the subject, with the goal of providing insights into the fundamental mechanisms driving the success of deep learning. We believe that a deeper understanding of the mathematical foundations of deep learning will enable researchers to approach its study with greater confidence. We hope that this work will inspire further exploration and advancement in this rapidly evolving field. Further reading recommendations and additional resources are provided at the end of the paper. We look forward to the continued growth and development of the rich and fascinating field of deep learning. Constructive cryptography offers a mathematical framework for analyzing and optimizing cryptographic protocols, focusing on the security provided by each component rather than the overall system. By treating protocols as algebraic objects, it facilitates the extraction of essential security features, including the identification of the minimal requirements for each cryptographic primitive. The approach has been particularly useful in developing private key encryption and private information retrieval algorithms with improved security and efficiency. This research aims to explore the benefits of an alternative paradigm, known as interactive constructive cryptography, which incorporates interactivity into the analysis of cryptographic primitives. By doing so, it has led to the development of more efficient updatable encryption schemes and private information retrieval protocols, offering superior security and performance. Furthermore, it has been shown that updatable encryption provides a unified framework for understanding the relationship between security and computational efficiency in both classical and quantum cryptography. The findings also demonstrate the potential of interactive constructive cryptography to be applied to other cryptographic protocols, such as attribute-based encryption schemes. Finally, it has been proposed that updatable encryption can be further enhanced by integrating it with attribute-based encryption, thus providing more robust and efficient private information retrieval protocols. The full details of these results are available in the authors' PhD thesis. To facilitate further research, the code for the proposed algorithms has been made publicly available on GitHub. This paper introduces CacheQL, a method for quantifying and pinpointing cache side-channel vulnerabilities in software. CacheQL leverages a novel query language that enables the expression of memory operations, allowing developers to specify side channels of their choice and pinpoint the specific parts of their code that may be vulnerable. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through CacheQL's application to the Apache HTTP Server, where it accurately identified a previously known vulnerability and, in addition, discovered a previously unknown vulnerability. Furthermore, using CacheQL, it was found that a significant portion of web applications are susceptible to cache side channels, highlighting the significant impact of CacheQL. GANs have become a widely accepted approach for data generation, but their practical application remains restricted due to the difficulty of training.  One major reason for this difficulty is mode collapse, which causes GANs to produce limited output samples, resulting in low diversity in generated data.  To address this challenge, researchers have proposed numerous strategies, but the underlying reasons for mode collapse are still unclear.  This study investigates the issue of mode collapse by examining the Hessian matrix of the generator, a matrix that represents the rate of change in the output of a complex function.  By analyzing the Hessian matrix, we can determine the stability of the output.  To investigate mode collapse, we conducted experiments using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets and observed the Hessian matrix's eigenvalues over time.  Our findings indicate that the collapse occurs when the Hessian eigenvalues become zero, suggesting that the generator's output has lost its stability.  Additionally, we found that the Hessian matrix's structure varies depending on the loss function used during training.  While the cross-entropy loss tends to produce a sparse Hessian matrix, the W-1 loss produces a denser matrix.  Our research offers new insights into the problem of mode collapse and suggests that analyzing the Hessian matrix can help us understand the underlying reasons for collapse.  This understanding can, in turn, enable us to develop more effective training strategies for GANs.  Our study provides empirical evidence that the Hessian matrix analysis can be used to identify and prevent mode collapse in GANs.  Our code for Hessian analysis is available on GitHub. In recent years, graph embedding techniques have been successfully applied to the analysis of complex networks, yielding significant advancements in the prediction of network topology. Nonetheless, the majority of these developments have focused on single-layer networks, whereas many real-world systems consist of multiple interconnected layers. This paper proposes a novel method, called MultiSAGE, which integrates the strengths of the SAGE approach with a unified framework for multi-layer networks. By employing a single optimization procedure, the method generates a unified representation of each layer within the network, enabling the recovery of the inter-layer connections. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through its application to three benchmark multiplex networks, the Gene Network, the Facebook social network, and the Kronecker graph. The results obtained using a leave-one-out approach reveal that MultiSAGE outperforms competing methods, including the SAGE approach applied individually to each layer. Furthermore, the method is shown to be robust in the presence of noise and reveals the underlying topology of the networks with high accuracy. In many real-world applications, positive and negative instances are scarce,
while examples with unknown labels are abundant, giving rise to the positive-
unlabeled (PU) learning challenge. This issue is often addressed using positive-
unlabeled training (PUNT) methods that utilize both positive and unlabeled
data to train predictive models. However, PUNT methods typically struggle with
highly imbalanced positive and unlabeled data, which can result in poor
performance. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel self-supervised
PUNT approach that leverages self-supervised positive and unlabeled data to
robustly learn from imbalanced PU data. By incorporating self-supervised
positive and unlabeled data, our method can effectively handle imbalanced
positive and unlabeled data, leading to improved performance. We also propose a
new self-supervised PUNT approach that utilizes self-supervised positive and
unlabeled data to handle highly imbalanced PU data, outperforming existing
methods in this area. Our proposed approach is evaluated on four real-world
datasets and shows significant promise for handling highly imbalanced PU data.

This approach utilizes a unique formulation that transforms the equations into a boundary value problem within each subdomain. This transformation is made possible by defining artificial boundary conditions that effectively mimic the behavior of the original problem. This allows for the application of existing solvers to solve the subdomain problems. Additionally, a set of boundary condition combinations has been identified to satisfy the continuity of the pressure across subdomains. This continuity is essential to match the pressure values at shared boundaries. Furthermore, a method for generating coarse initial subdomain partitions based on overlapping clusters has been implemented. This approach has been tested using various Stokes problems and shown to produce accurate solutions with optimal convergence rates. However, a detailed analysis of the convergence rates is limited to the rate of convergence in the $L^2$ norm for the velocity field. Further research is required to extend this analysis to the pressure field. This research has been conducted in the context of a 2D setting, and it remains to be seen whether similar results can be achieved in 3D settings. This is a topic of ongoing investigation. Reinforcement learning, a process of trial and error, is a widely applicable technique used in AI, machine learning, behavioral psychology, and neurobiology. It's a tool for AI to optimize movie recommender systems, for psychologists to develop treatment plans, and for biologists to study how organisms learn and adapt. Despite its diverse applications, reinforcement learning remains challenging to teach due to its varied uses and extensive scope. Existing teaching methods often rely on complicated simulations or in-depth knowledge of specific subjects like deep learning. 

This paper introduces Modular Object-Oriented Games (MOOGly), a framework for creating simple, machine-readable scenarios that can be applied across multiple disciplines. It's a tool for creating reproducible experiments, for researchers to test and validate their ideas, for educators to teach reinforcement learning techniques, and for students to engage with the material. 

The MOOGly framework includes a set of pre-built games that cover topics such as reinforcement learning fundamentals, learning models, and applications in education, psychology, and neuroscience. It also provides a set of tools for developers to create their own games. 

The MOOGly framework is designed to be accessible to a wide range of users, with a focus on the following groups: 

*   Researchers who want to test and validate their ideas in reinforcement learning.
*   Educators who want to teach reinforcement learning techniques.
*   Students who want to learn and practice reinforcement learning.
*   Practitioners who want to apply reinforcement learning to real-world problems.

This paper showcases the MOOGly framework through examples of how it's been used to teach reinforcement learning in AI, behavioral psychology, and neurobiology. It also highlights the framework's potential for educators, researchers, and practitioners. 

The paper concludes by discussing the limitations of the MOOGly framework and potential directions for future development.

The increasing reliance on digital platforms for recipe sharing has led to a proliferation of recipes online, although the manual and time-consuming process of collecting and verifying this information is a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose an innovative method for automatically generating recipes from a functional network-based framework. This approach involves creating a network of interconnected concepts and relationships, comprising entities such as ingredients, actions, tools, purposes, and cooking techniques. By applying natural language generation techniques to this network, we can produce diverse and varied recipes. To evaluate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted a comprehensive human assessment, examining the generated recipes from multiple angles and comparing them to those generated by a baseline model. The results demonstrate that our functional network-based approach outperforms traditional methods in producing coherent and grammatically correct recipes. Furthermore, human evaluators praised the novel recipes created by our system, highlighting its ability to provide new and inspiring culinary ideas. In contrast, the baseline model struggled to adapt to new data, producing repetitive and formulaic recipes that lacked originality. This work has significant implications for the automatic generation of novel recipes and may potentially revolutionize the way we interact with culinary knowledge and related products. To facilitate future research, we will release a comprehensive dataset of recipes and accompanying functional networks. This research paves the way for the development of intelligent cooking assistants that can provide users with novel and exciting recipe options. Experimental results have shown that the proposed method excels over existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both visual realism and accuracy. Furthermore, this research has also made available a dataset of diverse facial textures for further investigation and the development of future methods. Federated learning, a framework for distributed machine learning, has gained significant attention in recent years. It enables multiple entities to collaborate on training machine learning models without exchanging personal data. By combining the local models of these entities, the approach reduces data privacy risks associated with traditional machine learning methods. This paper introduces a new federated learning algorithm, called MKOLF, which optimizes model training by using multiple kernel models. By leveraging this approach, the method can effectively handle non-linear data and handle new incoming data streams. Our proposed method has been evaluated using real-world datasets and has shown comparable performance with other leading algorithms. Specifically, the results indicate that MKOLF achieves higher accuracy levels of up to 2.5%, with an average of 1.35% higher accuracy than other methods. Moreover, the method has been demonstrated to be efficient in handling new data streams with an average of 1.45% increased computation time. Overall, the results suggest that MKOLF is a promising approach for distributed machine learning applications. The primary objective of visualisation is to facilitate the human brain's rapid processing and interpretation of vast amounts of data. This goal necessitates the creation of effective visualisation tools that convey meaningful information through a combination of form, colour, texture, position, and other visual attributes. By doing so, these tools should avoid leading the viewer towards incorrect conclusions, instead allowing them to accurately comprehend the data. This concept is analogous to the principles of "Deceitful Visual Misdirections" and "Compelling Visual Representations" which aim to mislead or effectively engage the viewer. This article aims to discuss the distinction between the two approaches, as well as the principles underlying "Compelling Visual Representations". It also aims to provide practical insights and guidelines for designing effective visualisation tools that effectively engage the human brain. This discussion will be illustrated through various examples of compelling visualisation techniques. This article will be presented at the 2022 EuroVis/EGVE Conference. This study introduces a novel approach to translating source programming languages into target programming languages. Unlike other methods that solely focus on source-to-target translation, we explore the reverse process of target-to-source translation and leverage a grammar-based approach to tree transformation. By representing tree translation as a sequence-to-sequence task, we employ a tree-to-tree model that incorporates a parser and a translator. This model is evaluated on two translation tasks: Java-to-C++ and C-to-C++. This approach is based on theoretical predictions showing that higgsino final states tend to produce wide production angles, while top-antitop production has a much narrower angle distribution. By implementing basic angular cuts, the background signal ratio can be improved by nearly 20% for heavy higgsinos and about 30% for lighter ones. This technique is applicable to a broad range of collider parameters and can be used in conjunction with other methods to further reduce background noise. This setup includes a larger pseudorapidity range and advanced jet-detection capabilities, which would allow for more accurate identification of top-antitop production. By combining this with the proposed angular cuts, a significant reduction in background noise can be achieved. In this research, we introduce a novel, speaker-verified feature called Trainable MFCCs that enhances speaker recognition capabilities. By incorporating a trainable hidden Markov model into the Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient extraction process, we make the features fully optimizable for speaker verification tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that using Trainable MFCCs yields significant improvements in the accuracy of the Kaldi deep neural network-based speaker recognition system on the LibriSpeech and SLT corpora, surpassing non-trivial baseline performances. Notably, our results indicate that speaker verification systems can achieve comparable wER scores as automatic speech recognition systems. Additionally, our analysis reveals that Trainable MFCCs are particularly beneficial for smaller, less diverse datasets. We also examine the impact of Trainable MFCCs on the neural network's internal workings and find that it encourages more robust representations. Finally, our study explores the relationship between Trainable MFCCs and speaker embedding models, suggesting that Trainable MFCCs could be considered a type of speaker embedding model. However, our findings also indicate that using Trainable MFCCs in conjunction with a neural network speaker recognition system does not necessarily lead to overfitting. Overall, our research shows that Trainable MFCCs are a valuable addition to speaker verification systems. To address this issue, we investigate whether early crop production estimates derived from satellite imaging can serve as a viable alternative. Our study focuses on Senegal, a country with limited crop data, where early predictions based on satellite data could be a crucial tool for policymakers. To test this idea, we analyzed three crops—rice, maize, and cowpea—and found that while predicting these crops at a national level is challenging, it's possible to make more accurate predictions for specific regions. Our results suggest that maize and cowpea yields can be predicted with reasonable precision, while rice and rice varieties predictions face more significant uncertainties. The success of these predictions relies on various factors, including crop diversity, weather patterns, data availability, and existing crop data. Our findings suggest that high-resolution satellite data could potentially bridge data gaps in crop areas and provide valuable insights for more accurate predictions. The potential benefits of early crop yield predictions include improved policy decisions, enhanced agricultural research, and increased food system resilience. However, further research is needed to develop more accurate models and refine their precision. Our study contributes to the development of early crop yield forecasting systems and offers guidance for implementing these systems in developing countries. Feature switches are a key mechanism in enabling and disabling features within Go modules without altering the original code. This allows developers to easily switch between features without publishing updated modules. This research study examined feature switches in 14 prominent Go open-source projects hosted on GitHub. The results indicate that feature switches are frequently used in these projects, with over 1,700 switches detected in the analyzed dataset, which consisted of over 33,000 commits and 4,500 authors from 2016 to 2021. An analysis of the research findings revealed that feature switches are often linked to contributors and are more common in the Linux operating system context. Additionally, it was discovered that feature switches are more likely to be associated with merge operations and occur less frequently in the reviewed projects. An investigation into bug-fix commits related to feature switches was also conducted, which showed that these commits are relatively rare, with only a few percent of the studied commits being related to feature switches. The results indicate that these commits are less common to fix feature switch-related bugs. The research findings suggest that feature switches are an essential tool in the development process of Go open-source projects and are used effectively by developers to manage dependencies and implement new features. The study's outcomes can provide valuable insights for researchers and developers to better understand the role of feature switches in software development. Future research directions may involve exploring the adoption and usage of feature switches across various programming languages and in different software development contexts. Pandemics can have a profound impact on communities worldwide, necessitating immediate action to prevent widespread illness and death. In the early stages of a pandemic's spread, predictive models can help public health officials make informed decisions and allocate resources effectively. However, these models can be hindered by a lack of available data and time. To address these challenges, we've developed an adaptable framework that leverages available data to inform forecasting and outbreak response. This approach involves integrating multiple data sources to create a dynamic modeling pipeline that can be tailored to specific needs, from predicting disease spread to optimizing resource allocation and post-pandemic recovery efforts. By combining data from diverse sources, we've developed a versatile tool that can be applied across the pandemic spectrum, as demonstrated by its application in the COVID-19 pandemic. This work demonstrates the potential of a data-driven modeling approach in facilitating effective pandemic response and recovery strategies. Furthermore, we've made our source code and related tools publicly available to facilitate research, planning, and response efforts at the individual, community, and national levels. Our goal is to empower users to adapt and apply our modeling framework to specific contexts, with or without access to real-time data, and to explore new avenues for improving our understanding of pandemics. To this end, we've included a collection of example use cases and applications, as well as a set of tools and resources that can be used to replicate our work and explore new modeling approaches. By sharing our work, we aim to accelerate the development of robust and reliable modeling and data analysis capabilities for pandemic response and recovery. Finally, we've also included a set of recommendations for optimizing data collection and model development to improve our ability to predict and prevent future outbreaks. Overall, our work seeks to harness the power of data-driven modeling to improve our understanding of pandemics and inform effective response strategies at the individual and community levels. By doing so, we aim to reduce the risk of future outbreaks and promote post-pandemic recovery. Our approach involves a two-step process: first, we identify the relevant scene components using semantic segmentation and semantic segmentation-based grouping, and then we utilize a neural network to determine the precise camera movements required to execute the desired manipulation action. Our system is trained and tested on a real robot, comprising a Franka Emika Panda arm and an Intel Realsense D415 camera, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on a diverse range of objects, including some that resemble but are not identical to the training data. Additionally, we evaluate the method's generalizability to new objects, different environments, and unseen objects, and we examine its performance under varying camera resolutions and frame rates. Our results indicate that the method can successfully execute complex manipulations, such as picking and placing, opening, and closing, across a wide range of objects, and we discuss its performance and limitations. A new approach to developing highly accurate gradient boost trees for data-driven saliency detection is introduced in this paper. We have developed a novel approach to estimating the mass distribution of galaxy clusters using a trans-dimensional Markov Chain Monte Carlo method that combines sparse Bayesian inference with Gibbs sampling.
This approach allows us to model the mass distribution using a combination of a spatially independent Gaussian prior and a zero-mean inverse Gamma prior on its variance.
We have tested this method on simulated data and found that it can accurately recover the true mass distribution parameters, including the total mass of the cluster.
Our results indicate that the mass distribution can be recovered with high accuracy when the signal-to-noise ratio is greater than 1, and that the recovered mass profile is consistent with the true profile.
We also found that the recovered mass distribution is highly consistent with the total mass of the cluster when the total mass is known.
Our proposed method is a promising approach to estimating the mass distribution of galaxy clusters and can be easily adapted to other problems in weak lensing analysis.

Active learning strategies have garnered significant attention for reducing the need for labeled training data, but they often come at the cost of decreased test performance. A common issue with active learning is that the model can overfit the limited, labeled data, leading to a tradeoff between test performance and training efficiency. Our method involves using a pre-trained model to augment the training set, and then training it using the augmented data, which we term "test-enhanced" active learning. By leveraging this technique, we can attain higher test performance while still reducing the need for labeled data, as demonstrated through our experimental results. Our findings indicate that this method can achieve performance comparable to that of the fully supervised model with only 20% of the labeled data, and even outperform it under certain conditions. By separating the process of enhancing the training set from training the model, our technique offers a flexible and efficient solution to the active learning problem. In dynamic scenes, image restoration faces significant challenges stemming from motion blur, changing illumination, and other factors. Given the importance of image restoration in these situations, we aim to investigate its capabilities and limitations. Our research involves developing a range of image restoration methods, evaluating their performance on a diverse range of dynamic scene datasets, and comparing them to established techniques. We also introduce a new dataset of outdoor, dynamic scenes, designed to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of image restoration methods in a more challenging environment than typical indoor scenarios. Our findings highlight the importance of considering out-of-frame information in image restoration and suggest that further advances in this area may require the development of new, more effective image priors. We make our dataset and code available for public use. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of image restoration methods and provides a foundation for the development of more effective techniques in the future. We release our dataset and code publicly for use by others. More details can be found at https://vision.snu.edu/projects/DynamicImageRestoration. This study compares the performance of two factor models in predicting mortality, one with time-varying and the other with time-invariant factor loadings. By employing the Principal Component Model, we decompose actuarial mortality data into specific and factor components. The analysis utilizes a Bayesian framework to estimate specific mortality rates and factor loading proportions for 15 European countries over a 40-year period. The results reveal that models with time-invariant factor loadings perform as effectively as those with time-varying loadings in predicting mortality. However, the study suggests that models incorporating economic indicators such as fertility rates and GDP per capita perform better than those incorporating proxy indicators like temperature and the European Mortality Index. The study's findings are validated through a series of forecasting and out-of-sample tests, indicating that models with time-invariant factor loadings produce more accurate predictions. To optimize athletic performance and prevent injuries, monitoring heart rate during training is crucial.  A wearable device could provide this data, but it's not always available.  A computer vision approach could help by extracting heart rate information from video footage, enabling the estimation of a person's heart rate without requiring a wearable device.  This research focuses on predicting heart rate during strenuous exercise using videos, which poses a challenge due to motion, occlusions, and lighting changes affecting both the face and chest areas monitored in traditional wearable devices.  A new dataset featuring 1,323 videos of people performing various exercises has been created to support this research, which was tested using different machine learning models, which showed that a ResNet model performed best with a 14.5% mean absolute error. The problem of optimal shipping involves finding the most cost-effective way to transport goods from sources to destinations on a graph while meeting specified demand requirements. This complex issue can be simplified as a variant of a classic network flow problem. However, when dealing with a vast number of potential transportation paths, standard network flow algorithms become impractical due to their high computational complexity, which grows linearly with the number of paths. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a low-rank optimal shipping problem, which assumes that the optimal solution has a sparse structure. This assumption enables the development of an efficient algorithm that can be implemented in O(n^3) time, where n represents the number of paths. Furthermore, this work provides theoretical insights into the properties of optimal shipping solutions and derives a formula for the expected cost of optimal shipping under specific conditions. Additionally, an analysis of transportation costs for a real-world scenario involving a large number of ports and cargo shipments reveals that the optimal solution exhibits low rank. The paper also proposes a method to mitigate the effects of noisy input data on the solution structure. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the new algorithms in reducing computational time while achieving high accuracy compared to traditional methods. Specifically, our approach can process a large dataset in a fraction of the time taken by standard methods, while still maintaining a high level of accuracy. This study tackles the challenge of obtaining fair representations by combining mitigation and adversarial learning techniques to optimize representation fairness and utility simultaneously.  Two novel approaches, MSLFR-Mitigation and MSLFR-Stacking, are introduced to achieve this objective.  By employing the minimization of statistical disparity and equal opportunity metrics for MSLFR-Mitigation, and the combination of predictive error and fairness metrics for MSLFR-Stacking, both methods are able to learn fair representations.  Furthermore, MSLFR-Stacking is shown to outperform MSLFR-Mitigation by leveraging adversarial learning, while also offering superior performance compared to existing methods.  Additionally, MSLFR-Stacking is demonstrated to be more effective in handling fairness-utility trade-offs and achieving optimal utility when fairness is not a priority.  Experimental results on multiple datasets, including adult and compas, confirm the superiority of the proposed methods over baseline techniques.  By integrating adversarial learning with fairness mitigation and fairness-utility tradeoff, the proposed methods offer a more comprehensive approach to fair representation learning.  The code for these methods is available for public access.  The code can be found at https://github.com/zhengteng1995/Adversarial-Fair-Representation. A cutting-edge quantum system management framework leverages a reinforcement learning approach to optimize control of intricate systems with numerous quantum degrees of freedom. The DRLM framework represents a significant advancement in the application of machine learning to quantum system control. We've developed an approach that harnesses the power of unlabelled data by utilizing a sophisticated learner that collaborates with a learned observer. This observer is trained on labelled data and serves as a guide, providing the learner with a diverse array of potential hypotheses to work with. As a result, the observer's influence can be dynamically modulated in response to available data, allowing the observer to act as a minimalistic guide when data is scarce and a more authoritative one as data becomes more abundant. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this observer-assisted learning framework in the context of intent prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods, particularly when training data is limited. Furthermore, the observer's influence can be adjusted to strike a balance between accuracy and the cost of data collection. The observer itself can also be seen as a novel intent prediction model that outperforms existing models, even when trained in isolation. Additionally, our approach offers a novel perspective on the role of pre-training in intent recognition, highlighting the observer's ability to capture nuanced patterns in unlabelled data and leveraging this knowledge to improve intent prediction. The observer's guidance also enables the learner to avoid overfitting to limited data, allowing it to generalize better to unseen intents. To achieve energy-efficient acceleration of deep neural networks (DNNs), 
hybrid accelerators combine digital and in-memory accelerators, 
leveraging the strengths of each to optimize DNN inference. 
However, finding the optimal configuration of layers to assign between 
these accelerators is a complex task. This paper presents ENOS, a 
novel hybrid DNN accelerator framework that uses a two-stage search process 
to minimize energy consumption. First, ENOS uses a fast but less energy-efficient 
digital search to narrow down the possibilities. Then, it employs a more 
energy-efficient in-memory search process to identify the optimal configuration. 
ENOS's framework is designed to be adaptable to various DNN layers and 
accelerator architectures, and it has been successfully applied to a wide 
range of DNN models and architectures. The results show that ENOS outperforms 
other methods in terms of energy efficiency, with significant reductions in 
energy consumption of up to 24.6% and a 2.7 times faster search process. Furthermore, 
ENOS's framework can be easily extended to optimize other DNN accelerator frameworks. 
ENOS's source code is available for public use.

This paper outlines an AI system designed to solve the Tetris Link challenge, a high difficulty level in the popular puzzle game. The objective of Tetris Link is to utilize each piece of a given set within a larger board of a specified size. This can lead to difficulties in training, particularly when dealing with data that is both massive and fragmented.  To address these issues, a novel distributed reinforcement learning approach called distributed fragment-based reinforcement learning (DFRL) has been developed.  This method involves dividing data into smaller, localized subsets and training multiple agents in parallel to leverage their combined knowledge.  However, this approach also presents challenges in terms of coordination and communication costs.  To mitigate these issues, a distributed fragment-based reinforcement learning (MSRL) framework has been proposed, which utilizes a distributed architecture to reduce training overheads.  This framework has been tested on a real-world problem, the smart charging of electric vehicles, and has demonstrated its effectiveness in terms of efficiency and accuracy.  The results show that MSRL outperforms traditional reinforcement learning approaches by reducing training time and improving accuracy. The term Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has been increasingly used in recent years to describe methods for interpreting and justifying the workings of complex AI systems. Despite its growing prominence, there is a notable lack of a unified perspective on the subject. This paper aims to bridge the gap by providing an overview of the current state of XAI, drawing on both theoretical and practical insights. From a practical standpoint, we examine the key challenges faced in the field of XAI and identify key areas of research. From a theoretical perspective, we explore the connections between XAI and established fields such as artificial intelligence, philosophy, and statistics. Our analysis reveals that while progress has been made in recent years, significant work remains to be done in fully integrating a systematic approach to XAI within the broader framework of AI research. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of XAI by shedding light on the complex interplay between theoretical and practical perspectives within the field. This paper is intended as a starting point for a deeper dive into the subject, and we hope that it will serve as a valuable resource for researchers seeking to gain a comprehensive understanding of XAI. As such, we have made the paper openly accessible to the academic community. Comments and suggestions from readers are also highly welcome. methods often rely on specific algorithms like Policy Gradient Methods (PGMs)

principles of evolutionary algorithms and incorporates PGMs or DQN algorithms
as its fitness evaluation function. By combining these elements, our
approach enables the simultaneous optimization of both the policy and the
actions taken. We evaluate the performance of this method in various
scenarios, including non-stationary games and tasks, and compare it to other
state-of-the-art algorithms, showing that it outperforms them significantly.
Furthermore, our method's adaptability in response to environmental
changes is superior to other techniques, making it a promising tool for
real-world applications. The accompanying code is available for public use.

Our work reveals a flaw in the current definition of input stability, which necessitates a more comprehensive understanding of output stability. We propose a novel concept of input variation and introduce a framework for assessing explanation stability through the lens of output stability. Furthermore, our study identifies a critical connection between output stability and model interpretability, while also establishing a new benchmark for evaluating attribution-focused explanations using this input variation approach. Our research also highlights the limitations of existing methods, such as LIME and SHAP, and introduces a new algorithm called Input Variance Attribution that leverages our framework to provide more accurate and stable explanations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach using a range of models, datasets, and real-world examples, and show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of output stability. Our work provides a fresh perspective on the field of Explanatory Methods and sets the stage for a more nuanced understanding of input-output stability. By adopting this perspective, our research enables the development of more reliable explanations that can withstand slight variations in the input while maintaining their overall accuracy. In this research, we examine the nonlinear fracture dynamics of elastic materials with two distinct constitutive models. Firstly, we analyze a non-linear elastic material with a polynomial stress-strain relationship, where the fracture process is governed by a dynamic singularly perturbed boundary model. By applying the Griffith criterion, we demonstrate that in a two-dimensional setting, the fracture path exhibits an angular shape near the origin, and we establish a local asymptotic solution. Furthermore, we investigate the global asymptotic solution using a perturbation approach based on the boundary layer solution. Secondly, we consider an elastic material with a dynamic singular crack, where the fracture process is described by a constitutive model incorporating strain-limiting parameters. By applying the Griffith criterion, we derive a global solution for the crack problem, and we also analyze the evolution of the crack tip in time. Specifically, we explore the local Hamiltonian problem within a particular framework involving a graph where each edge is assigned a weight, and we analyze its behavior based on the minimum degree of the graph. Our findings indicate that this variant of the problem falls under the complexity class W[1] in parameterized terms. A substantial body of research has focused on the social and psychological effects of social media, particularly how it affects exposure to diverse perspectives. This paper explores a model of social media where users can choose to engage with opposing viewpoints, and investigates the optimal strategy for allocating these exposures to maximize learning. We develop an approach that combines dynamic programming and linear programming to solve large-scale problems efficiently, and our findings demonstrate significant gains in learning and reduction of biased opinions when users prioritize the dissemination of opposing viewpoints. Furthermore, our model reveals that a key determinant of effective exposure to adverse views is the average degree of bias among users, and that a simple, community-based strategy can yield optimal results under certain conditions. This research also identifies a critical assumption that may not hold in reality, and presents an alternative model that takes into account the potential negative consequences of being exposed to adverse views. Our simulations indicate that this negative consequence can substantially diminish the benefits of exposure to adverse views, and that a more nuanced approach is required to mitigate its impact. This paper also explores the implications of our findings for the design of social media platforms, and presents a new model that incorporates a mechanism to reduce the negative consequences of exposure to adverse views. Our simulations demonstrate that this approach can lead to substantial improvements in learning and reduced bias, and that a simple, community-based strategy can be effective in this context. Finally, our research highlights the importance of considering the potential negative consequences of exposure to adverse views and the need for alternative models that can better capture these dynamics.
